hooks.text: One cosmic structure of black holes spans four billion light-years.
One cosmic structure takes four billion years to cross.
This structure is too big for the rules of physics.

title: This Cosmic Giant Breaks the Rules of Physics
description: The Huge Large Quasar Group spans four billion light-years, making it the largest structure ever found in our universe.

beats.text: One cosmic structure of black holes spans four billion light-years.
beats.visual: Map of the Huge-LQG quasar distribution, Sloan Digital Sky Survey, 2013.
queries: Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxy map

beats.text: It's packed with 73 quasars, which are supermassive black holes spitting light.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of a luminous quasar powered by a supermassive black hole.

beats.text: Roger Clowes found this Huge Large Quasar Group back in 2013.
beats.visual: Sloan Digital Sky Survey 2.5-meter telescope at Apache Point Observatory.

beats.text: Cosmologists once assumed the entire universe was smooth and uniform.
beats.visual: All-sky map of the cosmic microwave background from the Planck satellite, 2013.

beats.text: But this massive wall of light breaks that fundamental law.
beats.visual: Computer simulation of the large-scale filament structure of the cosmic web.

beats.text: Crossing it at the speed of light would take four billion years.
beats.visual: Illustration of light traveling through deep space across massive galaxy clusters.

beats.text: Some experts think it's actually just a massive statistical fluke.
beats.visual: Chart comparing the Huge-LQG to smaller known galaxy clusters.
queries: Large-scale structure of the universe chart

beats.text: Nothing else in the universe rivals this structure of black holes.
beats.visual: Wide-field visualization of the observable universe's largest structures.

better_than_last: Applied the 'authority-anchoring' hypothesis by naming Roger Clowes and the University of Central Lancashire to ground the discovery's legitimacy.
